captions.instagram:
How does a fan work?

Tilted blades, a magnetic field that spins, and a breeze that cools you without cooling the air. Take a fan apart in 3D and see why half speed costs one eighth of the power.

→ A fan is a motor, a few tilted blades, a wire guard and a switch.
→ Each blade is tilted, so as it sweeps round it shoves air out of one side.
→ Spin it backwards and the same blades pull air up: winter mode.
→ Two sets of coils take turns, making a magnetic field that spins and drags the rotor round.
→ BLDC fans use magnets and electronics, and need less than half the power.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox-production-fd52.up.railway.app/fanclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How does a fan work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
Tilted blades, a magnetic field that spins, and a breeze that cools you without cooling the air. Take a fan apart in 3D and see why half speed costs one eighth of the power.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox-production-fd52.up.railway.app/e/fanclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/fanclear

In this video:
• A motor, blades, a guard and a switch. An electric fan is a motor with a hub of tilted blades on its shaft, a wire guard around them, and a switch or regulator to set the speed.
• Tilted blades push the air. Each blade is tilted, with its leading edge higher than its trailing edge.
• A magnetic field that turns. In an induction motor, two sets of coils are fed so their currents peak one after the other, thanks to a capacitor.
• Half the speed, one eighth of the power. Airflow grows in step with a fan's speed, the push it makes grows with speed squared, and the power it needs grows with speed cubed.
• It cools you, not the room. A fan does not lower the air temperature.
• A worm gear swings the head. Behind the motor, a worm on the shaft turns a worm wheel one tooth per turn.
